LESSON 5 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Attack Surface & Attack Vectors

The attack surface is every way in; an attack vector is the one that got used. Count the entries you forgot before you harden the one you remember.

Beginner3 min
Why this matters

The attack surface is everything an attacker can touch; the attack vector is the particular route they use. One is a measurement, the other is a story about how it happened.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • list the ways into a system you already run or use
  • distinguish the surface from a single vector
  • spot the entry point people forget: the one that is not yours

In plain English

A house has a front door, a back door, windows, a loft hatch, a letterbox and a chimney. All of that together is the attack surface: the total set of ways in.

If somebody climbs in through the kitchen window, that window was the attack vector: the one route actually used, on that night.

The surface is what you count and reduce. The vector is what you read about afterwards. Confusing them is why people harden the front door and leave the loft hatch open.

How it works

Every entry point you add — a login form, an API, an upload field, a plugin, a contractor's access — enlarges the surface. That is not an argument against building things. It is an argument for knowing what you added.

  • Each way in is a promise you have to keep: it must authenticate, validate, log and be patched.
  • Surface that nobody owns is the dangerous kind: an old staging server, a forgotten subdomain, a test key left in code.
  • You cannot reduce the surface to zero. You can make it smaller than last month, and you can know what is on it.

A useful habit: for every new feature, ask "what did we just expose?" before asking "does it work?".

A worked example

An imaginary small business with a website, counted honestly:

  • The public site and its login form.
  • The admin panel — the same site, a different path, often weaker.
  • The API the mobile app talks to.
  • The mailbox everyone uses for support and password resets.
  • Six employee laptops and the personal phones they check email on.
  • A third-party chat widget loaded from someone else's server.
  • A staging copy from last year, still online, still with the default admin password.

Seven entries, and a typical owner would have listed two. The last one is the important one: it is not something the business built recently, it is something it forgot.

The mistake most beginners make

Assuming the attack surface is only what your own team built. Third-party scripts, plugins, contractors and old staging environments are all part of it — and all of them are usually weaker than the thing you are carefully testing.

The second mistake is counting entries you can see and ignoring the ones you cannot: subdomains nobody remembers, an API version still serving requests, an old employee's account that still works.

Try it in two minutes

Take one service you use and list every way in, including the boring ones:

  • The main login page.
  • Any admin or staff area.
  • Anything that talks to it automatically — an app, a script, an integration.
  • The email address attached to it, which can reset the password.

Count how many of those you could not name from memory. Those are the ones to go and look at.

Practice / apply

Open a site you run or a service you use and list, on paper, every way in. Do not test anything you do not own.

Key takeaways

  • Attack surface is the total set of ways in; an attack vector is the one used.
  • Every entry point is a promise to authenticate, validate, log and patch.
  • The forgotten entries — staging, old keys, third-party scripts — are usually the weakest.
  • For every new feature, ask what it exposed before asking whether it works.
